inline.s: The characteristics of the world are ever-abiding.” Just as the Zhao Lun says:

The whirlwind levels the peaks and is ever still; the rivers rush on together yet do not flow; the dust of the wild horse flutters yet does not move; the sun and moon traverse the heavens yet do not revolve.

” (Translation: The fierce wind topples the mountains and is ever still; the rivers race on together yet do not flow; the dust is blown about yet does not move; the sun and moon pass across the sky yet neither rises nor sinks.)

The phrases in the passage, “the whirlwind levels the peaks,” “the rivers rush on together,” “the dust of the wild horse flutters,” “the sun and moon traverse the heavens,” describe the phenomenal marks (the marks of the world)

. Yet, seen in light of the real character of all dharmas, there are no whirlwind, no rivers, no wild horse, and no sun and moon at all (fundamentally nothing exists); how then could there be any leveling of peaks, rushing together, fluttering, or traversing the heavens? Therefore it is said: ever still, not flowing, not moving, not revolving. (For details see
The Real Character of All Dharmas
The Heart Sutra says:
“The empty character of all dharmas: neither arising nor ceasing, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing.”
(For the annotation see
A Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra

[Whirlwind] Also called pila (vairambha), translated as “great fierce wind.” This is the great fierce wind that arises at the time of the world-ending catastrophe. [World-ending catastrophe] The three catastrophes of fire, water, and wind that arise at the end of the kalpa of destruction; these three catastrophes sweep away the entire world. [The whirlwind levels the peaks] At the time of the world-ending catastrophe, the great fierce wind topples Mount Sumeru.

[Wild horse] A metaphor for dust. When spring arrives and the yang energy stirs, looking off toward the dust that rises among lakes and wilds resembles galloping horses, and so it is called “the wild horse.”

blocks.text: 7. Inner and Outer as a Single Whole

inline.s: [7. Inner and Outer as a Single Whole. This means that when one is at work on the practice, regarding the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the sun, moon, and stars, the inner body and the outer worlds, all dharmas whatsoever — all are the very substance of the true mind, serene and still, void and bright, without so much as a hairsbreadth of difference; the great chiliocosm and the worlds of dust are beaten into one whole; where could any deluded mind be found? Thus the Master Zhao said: “Heaven and earth share the same root with me, and the myriad things are one body with me.” This is the work, practiced within and without as a single whole, of extinguishing delusion.]

7. Inner and Outer as a Single Whole (inner and outer all become one body). When one is at work on the practice, the mountains, rivers, and great earth, the sun, moon, and stars, the inner body and mind and the outer worlds, all dharmas whatsoever — all are the very substance of the true mind, serene and still, void and bright, without so much as a hairsbreadth of difference. The great chiliocosm and all the worlds of dust are beaten into one whole; where could any deluded mind be found? Thus the great Master Sengzhao said: “Heaven and earth share the same root with me, and the myriad things are one body with me.” This is the work, practiced within and without as a single whole, of extinguishing delusion.

[World of things] The world of physical objects; this is a general term for the mountains, rivers, and great earth, houses, and all manner of implements and articles of use. It has the same meaning as the “world of material things.” [Chiliocosm of worlds] Great chiliocosms as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. [Chiliocosm] A thousand small worlds make one “small chiliocosm”; a thousand small chiliocosms make one “medium chiliocosm”; a thousand medium chiliocosms make one “great chiliocosm.” Because there are multiples of three thousands within it, the great chiliocosm is also called the “three-thousand-great-thousand world.”

blocks.text: 8. Inner and Outer as Complete Function

inline.s: [8. Inner and Outer as Complete Function. This means that when one is at work on the practice, one takes all dharmas whatsoever — inner and outer, body and mind, the worlds, and all actions and doings — and contemplates them all as the wondrous functioning of the true mind. The moment any thought arises it is the wondrous function appearing before one. Since everything is the wondrous function, where can the deluded mind settle? Thus Yongjia said: “The real nature of ignorance is precisely the Buddha-nature; this illusory empty body is precisely the Dharma-body.” The Song of the Twelve Hours of the Elder Zhigong says: “At the hour of dawn, the mad machine lies hidden in the Dao-body; whether sitting or lying, one knows not that this is the Way, but only bustles about toilsomely in suffering.” This is the work, practiced within and without as complete function, of stilling delusion.]

8. Inner and Outer as Complete Function. When one is at work on the practice, one takes all dharmas whatsoever — inner and outer, body and mind, the worlds, and all actions and doings — and contemplates them all as the wondrous function of the true mind. The moment any thought arises it is the wondrous function appearing before one. Since everything is the wondrous function of the true mind, where can the deluded mind settle? Thus Yongjia s Certificate of the Way says: “The real nature of ignorance is precisely the Buddha-nature; this illusory empty body is precisely the Dharma-body.” The Song of the Twelve Hours of the Elder Baozhi says: “At the hour of dawn, the mad machine lies hidden in the Dao-body; whether sitting or lying, one knows not that this is the Way, but only bustles about toilsomely in suffering.” This is the work, practiced within and without as complete function, of stilling delusion.
[Dawn] The early morning. [Yin] The yin hour (from three to five in the early morning). [Dawn, yin] This is the time when a cultivator of the Way rises.

[9. Substance and Function as One. This means that when one is at work on the practice, although one has silently merged with the true substance, a single flavor of emptiness and stillness, yet within it there is hidden a bright awareness — this is substance that is function; and within the bright awareness there is hidden emptiness and stillness — this is function that is substance. Thus Yongjia said: “What is mindful and still is right; what is mindful and deluded is wrong; what is still and mindful is right; what is indifferent and still is wrong.” Since within stillness there is no room for indifference, and within mindfulness no room for idle thinking, how can any deluded mind arise? This is the work, in which substance and function are one, of extinguishing delusion.]

9. Substance and Function as One. When one is at work on the practice, although one has quietly merged with the true substance, a single flavor of emptiness and stillness, yet within it there is hidden a bright awareness — this is substance that is function; and within the bright awareness there is hidden emptiness and stillness — this is function that is substance. Thus the great Master Yongjia said: “To be mindful and yet still is right; to be mindful and yet deluded is wrong; to be still and yet mindful is right; to be indifferent and still is wrong.” Since within stillness there is no room for indifference, and within mindfulness no room for idle thinking, how can any deluded mind arise? This is the work, in which substance and function are one, of extinguishing delusion.
[Mindful (
xing xing
)] Clear and alert in spirit. [Indifferent] Dull and sunk.

[10. Transcending Substance and Function. This means that when one is at work on the practice, one does not distinguish inner and outer, nor discern east, west, south, and north, but takes the four quarters and eight directions as a single great gate of liberation. Round and perfect, substance and function undivided, not the slightest leaking-through, the whole body beaten into one — where can any delusion arise? The ancients said: “The whole body has no crack or seam; above and below it is perfectly round.” This is the work, transcending substance and function, of extinguishing delusion.]

10. Transcending Substance and Function. When one is at work on the practice, one does not distinguish inner and outer, nor discern east, west, south, and north, but takes the four quarters and eight directions as a single great gate of liberation. Round and perfect, substance and function undivided, not a hair of leaking-through, the whole body beaten into one — where can the deluded mind arise? The ancients said: “The whole body has no crack or seam; above and below it is perfectly round.” This is the work, transcending substance and function, of extinguishing delusion.
[Crack or seam (
xia
)] A gap or fissure. [Very (
te
)] Too; exceedingly. [Perfectly round (
luan
)] Round in appearance; a reference to the full moon.

[Of the above ten methods of practicing, one need not use all of them. If but one method is brought to accomplishment, the delusion is extinguished of itself and the true mind appears. According to one s capacity and past habits, whichever method one has affinity with, practice that one. These practices are the work of no-effort, not an effort performed with a deliberate mind. This method of resting the deluded mind is the most essential, and therefore it has been spoken of at length; do not think it
(is)
prolix.]

Of the above ten methods of practicing, one need not use all of them. If only one method is brought to accomplishment, the delusion is extinguished of itself and the true mind appears. Therefore, following one s own capacity and past habits, whichever method one has had affinity with, adopt that method. These ten practices are the work of no-effort, not the effort of a deliberate mind. Since this method of resting delusion is the most essential, it has been spoken of at length; please do not feel it tedious.

blocks.text: 8. The Four Postures of the True Mind

inline.s: [The four postures] An abbreviation for the four deportments. [The four deportments] These are the rules that monks and nuns must observe, that is, being careful in the daily movements of daily life so as to maintain composure and dignity. The four deportments are: walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. One should walk like the wind, stand like a pine, sit like a bell, and lie like a bow.

[Someone asks: In what was said before about stilling delusion — is it only by sitting in meditation that one practices, or does it also extend to walking, standing, and lying down? The answer: The sutras and treatises speak mostly of practicing by sitting, because sitting makes success easy; but when one has practiced for long and gradually become proficient, one may also practice in walking, standing, and lying down.]

The questioner asks: In what was said before about stilling delusion — is it only by sitting in meditation that one practices, or can one also practice while walking, standing, and lying down? The answer: The sutras and treatises speak mostly of practicing by sitting, because sitting makes success easy; when one has sat in meditation for long and gradually become proficient, one may then also practice in walking, standing, and lying down.

[The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says: “If one cultivates calm-abiding, one should dwell in a quiet place, sit upright with right thought, not relying on the breath, not relying on forms and colors, not relying on emptiness, not relying on earth, water, fire, or wind, and even not relying on seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; all thoughts whatsoever are removed as soon as they arise, and the thought of removal itself is also cast away. Because all dharmas are originally without thought: thought after thought does not arise, thought after thought does not cease. Nor may one, after letting the mind go out to grasp an external realm, come to remove the mind by means of the mind. If the mind runs scattered, one should at once gather it back and abide in right thought. This right thought — know that it is mind-only, without any external realm; and this very mind likewise has no self-characteristic, for thought after thought is unobtainable.]

The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says: “If one cultivates calm-abiding, one should dwell in a quiet place and sit upright with right thought, not relying on the breath (not regulating the breath), not relying on forms and colors, not relying on emptiness, not relying on earth, water, fire, and wind, and even not relying on seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; all thoughts whatsoever are removed as soon as they arise, and the thought of removal is also cast away. This is because all dharmas are originally without thought: thought after thought does not arise, thought after thought does not cease. Nor may one let the mind go out to grasp an external realm and only then come to remove the mind by means of the mind. If the mind runs scattered, one should at once gather it back and abide in right thought. As to this right thought — know that all is mind-only, without any external realm, and this very mind also has no self-characteristic, because thought after thought is unobtainable.

[Cultivating calm-abiding] Doing the work of stilling deluded thoughts. [Seeing, hearing, sensing, knowing] A general term for the consciousness touching the external realm. The function of the eye-consciousness is “seeing,” of the ear-consciousness “hearing,” of the nose, tongue, and body consciousnesses “sensing,” and of the mental (sixth) consciousness “knowing.” [All thoughts whatsoever are removed as soon as they arise, and the thought of removal itself is cast away] “All thoughts whatsoever are removed as soon as they arise” is the work of bringing ten thousand thoughts to one. “Also casting away the thought of removal” is the work of bringing the one to nothing. [Nor may one, after letting the mind go out to grasp an external realm, come to remove the mind by means of the mind] Because to “remove the mind by means of the mind” in this way is to remove delusion with delusion, and to be swept along by delusion. This is the particular point to be careful of when doing the work of calm-abiding.

[If one rises from sitting and goes, comes, advances, and stops, doing whatever one does, at all times one should constantly bear in mind the skillful means and contemplate in accord with it. Practicing long and becoming proficient, the mind is able to abide. Because the mind abides, it gradually becomes sharp and keen, and following along it enters the samadhi of suchness, deeply subdues the afflictions, faith increases, and one quickly accomplishes the non-retrogressive. Only those who are doubtful, who do not believe and slander, those with heavy karmic obstructions, and the arrogant and indolent, are excepted. People such as these cannot enter it.” According to this, then the four deportments are all included.]

If one rises from the seat and goes out, comes in, advances, and stops, doing whatever one does, at all times one should use skillful means to contemplate according to conditions; if the mind runs scattered, one should at once gather it back and abide in right thought. Practicing long in this way and becoming proficient, deluded thoughts no longer arise (the mind is able to abide). Because deluded thoughts no longer arise (because the mind abides), the power of concentration gradually becomes ever more sharp and keen, and following along it enters the samadhi of suchness, deeply subduing the afflictions, faith increases, and one quickly accomplishes the non-retrogressive. Only those who are doubtful, who do not believe and slander, those with heavy karmic obstructions, and the arrogant and indolent are excepted. The samadhi of suchness cannot be entered by people such as these.” Based on this passage of the Treatise on the Awakening of Faith, it can be seen that the practice of stilling delusion in the true mind can be carried out in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

[The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “First rely on the Tathagata s practice of serenity, hold fast to the precepts, settle the assembly of disciples, and sit at ease in a quiet room.” This is the initial stage of practice. Yongjia said: “Walking is Chan, sitting is Chan; whether speaking or silent, moving or still, the body is at ease.” According to this, the four deportments are likewise included.]

The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “(Those who seek the Tathagata s pure and perfect enlightened mind should be of right thought and far from all illusions.) First one should cultivate calm-abiding (first rely on the Tathagata s practice of serenity), and for this one must hold fast to the precepts and settle the assembly of disciples, then sit at ease in a quiet room to practice.” This speaks of the initial stage of cultivating calm-abiding, which requires sitting in meditation. The great Master Yongjia said: “Walking is Chan, sitting is Chan; whether speaking or silent, moving or still, the body is at ease.” Based on this passage of instruction, it can be seen that the practice of stilling delusion in the true mind can be carried out in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down.

[Serenity (shamatha)] Translated into Chinese as “calm-abiding.” [Settle the assembly of disciples] To live in harmony with one s disciples and the great assembly. [Sit at ease] To sit silently and still.

[Summing up the merit of the practice: if while sitting one cannot still the mind, how much less can walking, standing, and lying down enter the Way? But for one who has used the practice to proficiency, though a thousand sages came they would not be startled into rising, though all manner of demons and heretics swarmed about he would not look back; how then could one be unable to practice in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down? It is like one who harbors hatred toward another: even while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, eating and drinking, in all actions, at all times he cannot forget it; and the one who loves another is likewise. Now hatred and love are matters of the concrete mind, and they can still be contained in the walking, standing, sitting, and lying down of the concrete mind; but the practice now is a matter of the no-mind. What doubt can there be that it would not constantly appear in the four deportments? I fear only that one will not believe and will not do it. If one only does it and believes it, then the Way within the deportments will surely not be lost.]

In sum, if in sitting still one cannot yet still the mind, how much less can one enter the Way while walking, standing, and lying down. But for one whose practice of stilling delusion in the true mind is used to proficiency, though a thousand sages came they would not startle him into rising, though all manner of demons and demons of every sort beset him, he would pay them no heed; how could it be that he cannot do the practice in walking, standing, and lying down? For example, if someone hates another, even while walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, eating and drinking, and in all his doings, at all times he cannot forget it; and one who delights in another is likewise. Moreover hatred and love are matters of the concrete mind, and they can find room within the concrete mind in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down. The present practice, though, is a matter of the no-mind; what need is there to doubt that the practice could not constantly appear before one in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down? I only fear that one will not believe and not do it. If one believes and does it, then the practice of stilling delusion within walking, standing, sitting, and lying down will surely not be lost.

[Someone says: When the deluded mind is stilled the true mind appears. But where now are the substance and function of the true mind? The answer: The wondrous substance of the true mind pervades all places. Yongjia said: “Never leaving the very spot, it is ever serene and still; seek it and you will know that it cannot be seen.” The sutra says: “Because of the nature of empty space, because it is ever unmoving, because in the Tathagata-store there is no arising and ceasing.” The great Fayan said: “Everywhere is the road to bodhi; every heading is the forest of merit.” This is where the substance is.]

The questioner asks: When the deluded mind is stilled the true mind appears. But where now are the substance and function of the true mind? The answer: The wondrous substance of the true mind pervades all places. The great Master Yongjia said: “(The true mind) never leaves the very spot, ever serene and still; seek it and you will know that it (the true mind) cannot be seen.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Because of the nature of empty space, because it is ever unmoving, because in the Tathagata-store there is no arising and ceasing.” The great Chan Master Fayan (Master Wenyi) said: “Everywhere is the road to bodhi; every heading is the forest of merit.” These all speak of where the wondrous substance of the true mind dwells.

[The wondrous function of the true mind appears in response to stimulus, like an echo answering a sound. Fadeng said: “From then to now it should not fall; clearly it is before the eyes. A wisp of cloud rises in the evening valley; a lone crane descends from the distant sky.” Thus Huayan of the Wei Prefecture said: “The Buddha Dharma is in daily use, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in drinking tea and eating rice, in the mutual exchange of words. Yet in what one does and does, when the mind is stirred to a single thought, it is no longer so.” From this we know that the substance pervades all places and can everywhere give rise to function; but because the presence and absence of conditions is unfixed, the wondrous function too is unfixed, though it is not that there is no wondrous function. Those who cultivate the mind, wishing to enter the sea of the unconditioned and ferry across birth and death, must not be deluded about where the substance and function of the true mind dwell.]

As for the wondrous function of the true mind, it appears in response to stimulus, like a mountain valley echoing a sound. The Chan Master Fadeng said: “From then to now it should not fall; clearly it is before the eyes. A wisp of cloud rises in the evening valley; a lone crane descends from the distant sky.” Thus the old Huayan of the Wei Prefecture, in the Pointing at the Moon Record, said: “The Buddha Dharma is in daily use, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, in drinking tea and eating rice, in the mutual exchange of words. Yet in what one does and does, the moment the mind is stirred to a single thought, it is no longer so.” From this we know that the wondrous substance of the true mind pervades all places and can everywhere give rise to function; but because the presence and absence of conditions is unfixed, the wondrous function is likewise unfixed, though it is not that there is no wondrous function. Those who cultivate the mind, wishing to enter the sea of the unconditioned and ferry across birth and death, must not be deluded about where the substance and function of the true mind dwell.

blocks.text: 10. The True Mind Transcends Birth and Death

inline.s: [Someone says: I have heard that one who has seen the nature leaves birth and death. Yet the patriarchs of old were see-the-nature people, and they all had birth and death; now I see that people in the world who cultivate the Way also have the matter of birth and death. How can it be said that one leaves birth and death?]

Someone asks: I have heard that one who has seen the nature leaves birth and death. Yet the patriarchs of old were see-the-nature people, and they all had birth and death; now I see that people in the world who cultivate the Way also have birth and death. How can it be said that one “leaves birth and death”?

[One who has seen the nature leaves birth and death] The statement “one who has seen the nature leaves birth and death” is not accurate; what is meant is: one who has destroyed the attachment to self (for example, an arhat) leaves birth and death. [Attachment to self] Also called attachment to a person, that is, deludedly grasping body and mind as a self. [Leaving birth and death] This does not mean that the present body will not die, but that after the end of this lifespan (the death of the body), the consciousness will not go on to be reborn, and so there will be no more death.
For example, one who has realized the fruit of arhatship: when this lifespan ends, the consciousness will not go on to be reborn, but abides in nirvana.

Another example: once a reciter of the Buddha s name is reborn in the Western Land of Utmost Bliss, one has the diamond indestructible body of the Tathagata, forever free of old age, sickness, all suffering, and death, right up to Buddhahood. [Nirvana] The realm of liberation and unconditioned-ness free of birth and death and of affliction.
[It is said: Birth and death originally do not exist; they are delusively taken to exist. It is like one with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky
(flowers)

. Or one without the disease says: there are no flowers in the sky. The sick one does not believe it. When the eye disease is gone the sky-flowers destroy themselves, and only then does he believe the flowers are nonexistent. Even while the flowers have not yet ceased, they are also empty; but the sick man delusively grasps them as flowers, not that they really exist in substance.]
Answer: Birth and death originally do not exist; they are only delusively counted as existent. It is like a man with diseased eyes seeing flowers in the sky (
the sky-flowers
). One without eye-disease says to him: there are no flowers in the sky. The sick man does not believe it. When his eye-disease is cured, the sky-flowers he sees
in the sky
naturally vanish, and only then does he believe there are no flowers in the sky. In the final analysis, the sky-flowers
in the sky
were never extinguished (because they had never arisen
at all
, how could one speak of their extinction?), for the sky-flowers
in the sky
do not exist; this is nothing but the diseased man s delusion, thinking there are flowers there; they are not really existent.

[Birth and death originally do not exist; they are delusively taken to exist] Birth and death are an affair of the dream of transmigration, and originally do not exist. Yet the ordinary man delusively grasps body and mind as a self, and so when this lifespan ends he goes again to take rebirth and has another body. Where there is birth there must be death; if in this life one continues to delusively grasp body and mind as self, then after death one must go again to take rebirth and have yet another body. Thus birth and death revolve without end. Cultivation is to cut off this attachment to self, this delusively grasping body and mind as a self. Once the attachment to self is cut off, when this lifespan ends the consciousness will not go on to be reborn, and so there will be no more death.

[It is like one who delusively takes birth and death as existent; or one without birth and death tells him: originally there is no birth and death. When one day that person s delusion ceases, birth and death destroy themselves, and only then does he know that birth and death originally do not exist. Even while birth and death have not yet ceased, they are likewise not really existent, because birth and death are delusively taken to exist.]

It is the same with one who is deluded in the dream of transmigration, delusively taking birth and death as existent. When an awakened person (one without birth and death) tells them that originally there is no birth and death, they absolutely will not believe it. But if one day they awaken (the delusive attachment ceases), then birth and death destroy themselves (they leave birth and death), and only then do they know that birth and death originally do not exist. Only while the delusive attachment has not yet ceased is birth and death likewise not really existent; and this is nothing but the delusive attachment (as with eye-disease) giving rise to birth and death (delusively seeing the sky-flowers).
[The awakened person] The Certificate of the Way says:
“In the dream there are clearly the six destinies; after awakening it is utterly empty, without the great chiliocosm.”

Thus, when the arhat s deluding karma of birth and death is exhausted, he no longer receives a future existence (he no longer receives a body in a future life). So after their passing into nirvana there is no more birth and death.

[The sutra says: “Good son, all sentient beings from the beginningless past have had all manner of inverted views, like a deluded man who confuses the four directions, delusively taking the four great elements as the self-characteristics of the body and the shadow-images of the six sense-objects as the self-characteristics of the mind, just as the diseased eye sees flowers in the sky. Even as the mass of sky-flowers vanishes into empty space, one cannot say that there is a definite place of their extinction. Why? Because there is no place of arising. All sentient beings, in that which is unarisen, delusively see arising and ceasing; therefore they are said to turn in the wheel of birth and death.”]
The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
All sentient beings, from the beginningless
past, have all manner of inverted views, taking illusory forms as real,
like
a man who has lost his direction, mistaking north for south
and east for west
delusively taking the body formed of the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind as the self-characteristics of the body, and
the thoughts
arising from the six roots touching the six sense-objects
as the self-characteristics of the mind. This is like
the diseased eye
seeing flowers, delusively seeing flowers in the sky. And even
when the eye-disease is cured, and
the mass of sky-flowers vanishes into empty space
one cannot
say
that they
have a
definite
place of
extinction.
Why
Because they are illusions and
have no place of arising
(they never arose, so how could there be a place of arising?)
. All sentient beings, in that which is unarisen, delusively see arising and ceasing,
and this delusory seeing of arising and ceasing is what is called
turning in the wheel of birth and death.

[The four great elements] All physical matter in the world is composed of the four elements of earth, water, fire, and wind, and so they are called “great”: the great earth, the great water, the great fire, and the great wind. Earth is of the nature of solidity, water of wetness, fire of warmth, wind of movement. [The shadow-images of the six sense-objects] That is,
thoughts.
When the six roots touch the six sense-objects, all manner of thoughts arise, and these thoughts are all illusory and unreal, and so they are called the shadow-images of the six sense-objects —
the
illusory images
that appear when the six
roots
touch the six sense-objects.
[Sky-flowers] That is, flowers in the sky. “Hua” in old usage is the same as “flower.”

[Based on this scripture passage, one may be certain that having realized the perfect enlightenment of the true mind, one understands that there is originally no birth and death. Now knowing that there is no birth and death, yet being unable to escape birth and death — that is because the practice is still insufficient.]

Based on this scripture passage, being certain that one has realized the perfect enlightenment of the true mind, one will understand that there is originally no birth and death. Those who now know that there is no birth and death yet cannot escape it — that is simply because their practice is still insufficient!

[Being certain of the realization of the true mind of perfect enlightenment, that there is originally no birth and death] Once one is certain of having realized the true mind of perfect enlightenment, one understands that there is originally no birth and death. Therefore, for one who has realized the true mind of perfect enlightenment, the birth and death of the six destinies is indeed an illusion; and if the delusive attachment
(grasping body and mind as self — attachment to self)

ceases, then after their passing into nirvana the self-nature (consciousness) will not go into the six destinies to take rebirth, and so leave birth and death. To understand that there is no birth and death is to cut off delusion as to views; for the delusive attachment to cease is to cut off delusion as to thought. Therefore to escape birth and death one must cut off both delusion as to views and delusion as to thought. [Delusion as to views and delusion as to thought] Delusion as to views and delusion as to thought. Delusion as to views is the confusion and error of the ordinary man in the sphere of views, such as the five perverse views of the view of self, the view of extremes, the perverse view, the view of holding to views, and the view of holding to precepts. Delusion as to thought is the confusion and error of the ordinary man in the sphere of thought, such as the afflictions of greed, anger, delusion, pride, and doubt. These two delusions are the root cause of sentient beings falling into the three worlds and vainly undergoing birth and death; cut them off and one can end birth and death and leave the three worlds. For example, in the vehicle of the hearers, cutting off delusion as to views realizes the fruit of stream-enterer; then, in the course of cutting off delusion as to thought, there are successively the three stages of once-returner, non-returner, and arhat. When delusion as to thought is fully cut off, one realizes the fruit of arhatship and leaves birth and death.

Therefore it is said in the teachings: The woman Amba asked Manjushri, “Clearly knowing that birth is a Dharma of non-birth, why is one still swept along by birth and death?” Manjushri said: “Because the power is not yet sufficient.” Later the master of Jinshan asked the master of Xiu, “Clearly knowing that birth is a Dharma of non-birth, why is one still swept along by birth and death?” Xiu said: “The bamboo shoot will in the end become a bamboo; but as now, can the shoot be split into bamboo strips for use?”]
Therefore, as the sutras and treatises say: The woman Amba asked the Bodhisattva Manjushri, “Clearly knowing that birth is a Dharma of non-birth, why is one still swept along by birth and death

” The Bodhisattva Manjushri answered: “This is because the power to extinguish the delusive attachment is not yet sufficient.” Later the master of Jinshan asked the master of Xiu, “Clearly knowing that birth is a Dharma of non-birth, why is one still swept along by birth and death
” The master of Xiu answered: “Although the bamboo shoot will in the end grow into a bamboo, yet as now, can the shoot be split into bamboo strips for use?”
[Master of the mountain] The lord of a mountain, an honorific title for the abbot of a monastery.
Clearly knowing that there is no birth and death, yet still being swept along by birth and death — this is because the
power to extinguish the delusive attachment
is not yet sufficient, and therefore after death the
self-nature (consciousness)

will still undergo the birth and death of the six destinies. Therefore, in one s study and practice, cultivating the power to extinguish the delusive attachment is of the utmost importance. The power to extinguish the delusive attachment is composed of two parts: the power of wisdom and the power of concentration. The power of wisdom can know the illusion; the power of concentration can leave the illusion. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says:
“To know the illusion is already to leave it; no need for contrivance. To leave the illusion is already to awaken; there are no gradual stages.”
Question: How does one cultivate the power of wisdom and the power of concentration?
Answer: Wisdom is born of concentration. Doing the work of “bringing ten thousand thoughts to one” and “bringing the one to nothing” (see
Awareness Chan

in the chapter “Probing Presence in Chan”) not only cultivates the power of concentration, but also cultivates the power of wisdom. In daily life one should at all times and in all places use the power of wisdom to know the illusion, and use the power of concentration to leave the illusion, holding wisdom and concentration in equal balance.

[Therefore, to know that there is no birth and death is not as good as to realize in body that there is no birth and death; to realize in body that there is no birth and death is not as good as to be merged in that there is no birth and death; to be merged in that there is no birth and death is not as good as to use that there is no birth and death. The people of today do not even know that there is no birth and death, much less realize it in body, be merged in it, or use it! Therefore those who grasp birth and death do not believe in the Dharma of no-birth-and-death; is that not understandable!]

Therefore, to know that there is no birth and death is not as good as to realize in body that there is no birth and death; to realize in body that there is no birth and death is not as good as to be merged in that there is no birth and death; to be merged in that there is no birth and death is not as good as to use, amid conditions, that there is no birth and death. The people of today do not even know that there is no birth and death, much less realize it in body, be merged in it, or use it amid conditions! Therefore, those who grasp birth and death do not believe in the Dharma of no-birth-and-death, and this too is understandable!
(Original title: True Mind, Primary and Auxiliary)

[Someone says: As said before, when the delusion is stilled the true mind appears before one. But when the delusion has not yet been stilled, is it only the no-mind work of resting the delusion, or is there another method to counter all the delusions? The answer: Primary and auxiliary are different. To still the delusion with no-mind is the primary practice; to cultivate all good is the auxiliary. It is like a bright mirror covered with dust: though one rubs it with the strength of the hand, one needs a wondrous medicine to polish it before the bright light appears. The dust is the afflictions. The strength of the hand is the no-mind work. The polishing medicine is all good. The mirror-light is the true mind. The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says: “Moreover, as to making the aspiration for those who have accomplished faith — what mind does one make? Briefly there are three kinds. What are the three? First, the straight mind: being of right thought of the Dharma of suchness. Second, the deep mind: accumulating all good practices. Third, the mind of great compassion: desiring to pull out the suffering of all sentient beings.”]

Question: As said before, when the deluded mind is stilled the true mind appears before one. If the deluded mind has not yet been stilled, is one only doing the no-mind work to still the delusion, or is there another method to counter all the delusions? Answer: Primary practice and auxiliary practice are different. One should take the no-mind stilling of delusion as the primary practice, and the cultivation of all good as the auxiliary. For example, when a bronze mirror is covered with dust and grime, although one rubs it with the strength of the hand, one still needs a wondrous medicine to polish it before the mirror-light appears. The dust and grime are the afflictions. The strength of the hand is the no-mind work. The polishing medicine is all good. The mirror-light is the true mind. The Treatise on the Awakening of Faith says: “Moreover, as to making the aspiration for those who have accomplished faith — what mind does one make? Briefly there are three kinds. What are the three? First, the straight mind, because of right thought of the Dharma of suchness. Second, the deep mind, because of accumulating all good practices. Third, the mind of great compassion, because of desiring to pull out the suffering of all sentient beings.”
